world_wide_web_day.label: World Wide Web Day
world_wide_web_day.intro: A nod to the invention that turned a network of computers into something everyone could browse. One day a year to remember that links, pages and bookmarks were once a brand new idea.
funFacts: Tim Berners-Lee wrote his proposal for the web at CERN in March 1989; his boss famously called it 'vague but exciting'.
The first web server was a NeXT computer carrying a handwritten label: 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!'
In 1993 CERN released its original web software into the public domain, helping the web spread.

ice_cream_sandwich_day.label: National Ice Cream Sandwich Day
ice_cream_sandwich_day.intro: Ice cream, squeezed between two biscuits, eaten with your fingers. The most portable dessert of the summer gets its own date in the middle of the hottest month.
funFacts: Pushcart vendors in New York were selling ice cream sandwiches for a penny each around 1899.
Australia has its own classic, the vanilla slice between wafers, while San Francisco is proud of its oatmeal-cookie It's-It.
The wafers are baked deliberately soft so your teeth go through them instead of squeezing the ice cream out of the sides.

watermelon_day.label: National Watermelon Day
watermelon_day.intro: The fruit that makes a picnic feel like a picnic. Sticky fingers, a slice the size of your face and a competition over who can spit the seeds furthest.
funFacts: A watermelon is about 92 percent water, which is exactly why it works so well on a hot afternoon.
Botanically it is a berry, a type called a pepo, with a hard rind and a soft fleshy centre.
Zentsūji’s square watermelons grow inside moulds and are harvested unripe as decorative objects.

chocolate_chip_cookie_day.label: National Chocolate Chip Cookie Day
chocolate_chip_cookie_day.intro: Golden edges, a soft middle and pockets of melting chocolate. A day for the biscuit that nearly every home baker attempts at least once.
funFacts: Ruth Graves Wakefield created the cookie at her Toll House Inn in Massachusetts in the 1930s.
She later let Nestlé print her recipe on their packaging, and the company began selling chocolate in ready-made chips.
Massachusetts made the chocolate chip cookie its official state cookie in 1997 after a campaign by schoolchildren.

traffic_light_day.label: International Traffic Light Day
traffic_light_day.intro: Red, amber, green: three lamps that quietly organise the whole planet's traffic. A day to appreciate the least glamorous and most useful invention on any street corner.
funFacts: The first electric traffic signal went into service on 5 August 1914 in Cleveland, Ohio, at the corner of Euclid Avenue and East 105th Street.
London had a gas-lit signal outside Parliament back in 1868, but it exploded a year later and injured the constable operating it.
Red light has a longer wavelength than blue light.

root_beer_float_day.label: National Root Beer Float Day
root_beer_float_day.intro: A scoop of vanilla ice cream dropped into a glass of root beer, and the foam does the rest. Cheap, noisy and wonderfully theatrical.
funFacts: The drink is credited to Frank J. Wisner, who mixed it in Cripple Creek, Colorado, in 1893 and called it a Black Cow.
The foam happens because the ice cream's fat and proteins trap the escaping carbon dioxide in tiny stable bubbles.
Root beer was traditionally flavoured with sassafras root, which US regulators banned as a food additive in 1960.

lighthouse_day.label: National Lighthouse Day
lighthouse_day.intro: A tip of the cap to the towers that stand in the weather so sailors don't have to guess where the rocks are. Few buildings are as photogenic or as stubborn.
funFacts: The date recalls 7 August 1789, when the US Congress took the country's lighthouses into federal care.
The Pharos of Alexandria was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and stood for roughly 1,500 years.
Augustin-Jean Fresnel's stepped lens of 1822 let a single lamp throw a beam far out to sea instead of wasting it on the sky.

international_cat_day.label: International Cat Day
international_cat_day.intro: The day belongs to the housemate who pays no rent, sleeps on the warm laptop and still gets away with everything. Cat people need no further excuse.
funFacts: Cats sleep between twelve and sixteen hours a day, spread over dozens of short naps rather than one long night.
Whiskers are roughly as wide as the cat and work as feelers for judging whether a gap is passable.
Ancient Egypt honoured the cat goddess Bastet, and mummified cats have been found by the thousand at her temple sites.

book_lovers_day.label: Book Lovers Day
book_lovers_day.intro: Permission to ignore your inbox, find a quiet corner and read for the pleasure of it. Paper, e-ink or audio, nobody is checking.
funFacts: Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time is often listed as the longest novel ever published, at well over a million words.
The Library of Congress holds around 178 million items and adds thousands more every working day.
Roughly 180 copies of the Gutenberg Bible were printed in the 1450s; about 49 still survive, most of them incomplete.

world_lion_day.label: World Lion Day
world_lion_day.intro: A day for the big cat that turns up on coats of arms, football crests and bedtime stories all over the world. Impressive from a safe distance, magnificent in a photograph.
funFacts: A lion's roar can carry about eight kilometres and is used to mark territory and locate the rest of the pride.
Lions are the only cats that live in real social groups; a pride is usually built around related females.
The lionesses do most of the hunting, often in coordinated teams, while the mane mainly signals a male's condition.

hip_hop_day.label: Hip Hop Day
hip_hop_day.intro: Turntables, a microphone, a piece of cardboard and a spray can: four elements that grew out of one Bronx party into a global culture. This is the date fans treat as its birthday.
funFacts: On 11 August 1973 DJ Kool Herc played a back-to-school party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, now widely called hip hop's birthplace.
His trick was the break: two copies of the same record, looping the drum passage so dancers never had to stop.
In 2021 the US Senate formally designated 11 August as Hip Hop Celebration Day.

world_elephant_day.label: World Elephant Day
world_elephant_day.intro: The largest land animal on the planet gets a day of its own. Elephants are clever, sociable and, judging by every zoo queue ever, endlessly fascinating to watch.
funFacts: An elephant's trunk contains tens of thousands of muscle units and can both uproot a tree and pick up a single leaf.
Those enormous ears are radiators: blood flowing through them cools down before returning to the body.
Elephant pregnancies last around 22 months, the longest of any land mammal.

lefthanders_day.label: International Lefthanders Day
lefthanders_day.intro: For everyone who smudges their own handwriting, fights with tin openers and sits at the wrong end of the dinner table. A day to point out that the world is built slightly wrong.
funFacts: Roughly one in ten people is left-handed, and the share is fairly stable across countries and centuries.
The day was first marked in 1976 by Dean R. Campbell, founder of the group Lefthanders International.
Left-handers are unusually successful in fencing, boxing and table tennis, where opponents rarely get to practise against them.

world_lizard_day.label: World Lizard Day
world_lizard_day.intro: Sun-warmed rocks, quick sideways glances and a tail that vanishes round a corner. A day for the reptiles most of us have only ever met on a holiday wall.
funFacts: There are more than 7,000 known lizard species, from thumb-sized geckos to the three-metre Komodo dragon.
Gecko toes are covered in millions of microscopic hairs that grip smooth glass using molecular attraction alone.
Many lizards can shed their tail to escape a predator and grow a replacement, though it is usually shorter and made of cartilage.

relaxation_day.label: National Relaxation Day
relaxation_day.intro: An official excuse to do nothing in particular. No chores, no productivity tips, just a hammock, a bench in the shade or a long afternoon nap.
funFacts: The hammock reached Europe from the Caribbean; the word comes from the Taíno hamaca via Spanish sailors.
Siesta comes from the Latin hora sexta, the sixth hour after sunrise, which is roughly the middle of the day.
Sleep researchers find naps of ten to twenty minutes leave you alert, while longer ones tend to leave you groggy.

roller_coaster_day.label: National Roller Coaster Day
roller_coaster_day.intro: The drop, the scream, the wobbly walk back to the exit. A day for the ride that people queue an hour for in order to be terrified for ninety seconds.
funFacts: The date marks 16 August 1898, when Edwin Prescott patented a coaster design with a vertical loop.
The ancestors were the Russian ice slides of the 18th century, wooden hills near St Petersburg covered in ice.
Coney Island's Switchback Railway of 1884 cost five cents and reached a top speed of about ten kilometres per hour.

thrift_shop_day.label: National Thrift Shop Day
thrift_shop_day.intro: A day for rummaging: worn-in jackets, odd crockery, a paperback someone loved before you. The joy is in the hunt, and the price tag rarely hurts.
funFacts: Goodwill grew out of a Boston mission founded in 1902, where donated clothes were repaired and resold by the people who needed the work.
The Salvation Army was collecting and reselling household goods through its salvage brigades before 1900.
Wool, cotton and denim all keep their structure for decades, which is why old clothes so often outlast new ones.

bad_poetry_day.label: Bad Poetry Day
bad_poetry_day.intro: Write something dreadful, rhyme moon with spoon and read it aloud without apology. The point is that nobody has to be good at it to enjoy it.
funFacts: William McGonagall of Dundee is routinely called the worst poet in the English language, and his readings drew crowds for exactly that reason.
His Tay Bridge Disaster is still quoted for lines that scan badly and rhyme worse.
Douglas Adams invented Vogon poetry as the third worst in the universe, with an audience tied to uncomfortable chairs.

world_photography_day.label: World Photography Day
world_photography_day.intro: From glass plates to the phone in your pocket. A day to notice that we all carry a camera capable of things a 19th-century studio could only dream of.
funFacts: On 19 August 1839, the details of the daguerreotype process were publicly presented in Paris.
The oldest surviving photograph from nature, Nicéphore Niépce's View from the Window at Le Gras, needed an exposure of many hours.
Early portrait sitters used head clamps to stay still, which is part of why nobody in old photographs looks relaxed.

radio_day.label: National Radio Day
radio_day.intro: The medium that survived television, cassettes and streaming and still keeps people company in the kitchen and the car. A day for crackling frequencies and familiar voices.
funFacts: KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcast US election results on 2 November 1920, an event usually called the first commercial radio broadcast.
Marconi reported receiving a signal across the Atlantic in 1901, at a time when physicists doubted radio waves could follow the curve of the Earth.
Orson Welles's 1938 War of the Worlds broadcast is famous less for the panic it caused than for how the story of that panic grew.

spumoni_day.label: National Spumoni Day
spumoni_day.intro: Three coloured layers of Italian ice cream, studded with candied fruit and nuts and cut into slices like a cake. A dessert that arrives looking like a celebration.
funFacts: Spumoni comes from Naples and traditionally combines chocolate, cherry and pistachio layers.
The name is related to spuma, Italian for foam, a nod to how much air is whipped into the cream.
Italian immigrants brought it to the United States in the 19th century, where it became a fixture in Italian-American restaurants.

eat_a_peach_day.label: National Eat a Peach Day
eat_a_peach_day.intro: Late August is peak peach season, so the instruction is simple: find a ripe one, lean forward and let it drip. Anything else would be a waste.
funFacts: Peaches were domesticated in China thousands of years ago and reached Europe via Persia, which is why the Latin name means Persian apple.
The peach belongs to the rose family and is a close relative of the almond; the kernel inside the stone looks the part.
A nectarine is not a hybrid but a peach with a single gene variant that leaves the skin smooth.

ride_the_wind_day.label: National Ride the Wind Day
ride_the_wind_day.intro: A day for anything that stays up because the air is moving: gliders, kites, paragliders and the occasional very determined pedal-powered aircraft.
funFacts: On August 23, 1977, Bryan Allen pedalled the Gossamer Condor around the required figure-eight course to win the Kremer Prize.
The aircraft weighed about 32 kilograms, less than the pilot, and won designer Paul MacCready the £50,000 Kremer Prize.
Gliders climb by circling in thermals, columns of warm rising air that soaring birds have used for far longer than we have.

strange_music_day.label: International Strange Music Day
strange_music_day.intro: Play something you would never normally play, or listen to a record that makes no sense to you. The rule for the day is simply that it must be unfamiliar.
funFacts: The day was started in 1998 by the New York musician Patrick Grant.
The theremin, built by Leon Theremin around 1920, is played by moving your hands near two antennas without ever touching it.
John Cage's prepared piano turns an ordinary grand into a percussion set by wedging screws and rubber between the strings.

banana_split_day.label: National Banana Split Day
banana_split_day.intro: A banana lengthwise, three scoops, sauce, cream and a cherry on top. Absurdly over the top, which is exactly the point.
funFacts: The split is credited to David Strickler, a 23-year-old apprentice pharmacist in Latrobe, Pennsylvania, in 1904.
It cost ten cents at a time when a regular sundae went for five, and students from a nearby college spread the word.
The classic version pairs chocolate, vanilla and strawberry ice cream with chocolate, pineapple and strawberry sauces.

dog_day.label: National Dog Day
dog_day.intro: For the friend who is delighted every single time you come home. A day for long walks, extra treats and far too many photographs.
funFacts: Dogs were the first animals humans domesticated, thousands of years before farming began.
A dog's nose print is as individual as a human fingerprint, and some registries use it as identification.
The area of a dog's brain devoted to smell is proportionally far larger than ours, which is why tracking work comes so easily.

rock_paper_scissors_day.label: World Rock Paper Scissors Day
rock_paper_scissors_day.intro: The fairest decision-making tool ever invented, available anywhere, requiring nothing but two hands. Best of three, and no arguing afterwards.
funFacts: The game reached the West from Japan, where it is called janken; its ancestors are Chinese hand games described centuries earlier.
In 2005 a Japanese company chose between Christie's and Sotheby's for a major art sale by having them play rock paper scissors.
Because people rarely play randomly, tournament players study opponents' habits; beginners open with rock more often than chance would suggest.

read_comics_in_public_day.label: International Read Comics in Public Day
read_comics_in_public_day.intro: Take the comic out of the house, sit on a bench and read it where people can see. The whole idea is to stop treating panels and speech bubbles as a private pleasure.
funFacts: The day was launched in 2010 and set on 28 August, the birthday of the artist Jack Kirby.
Kirby co-created Captain America, the Fantastic Four and the X-Men, and drew tens of thousands of pages in his career.
A copy of Action Comics #1 from 1938, the first appearance of Superman, has sold for several million dollars.

more_herbs_less_salt_day.label: More Herbs, Less Salt Day
more_herbs_less_salt_day.intro: A cheerful nudge to reach for the basil, thyme and parsley before the salt cellar. Food gets more interesting, not less, when you swap one for the other.
funFacts: Basil, mint, rosemary, sage and thyme all belong to the same family, recognisable by their square stems.
Rosemary's botanical name comes from the Latin ros marinus, sea dew, after the coastal cliffs where it grows wild.
Dried herbs are more concentrated by volume than fresh ones, so recipes usually call for about a third as much.

frankenstein_day.label: Frankenstein Day
frankenstein_day.intro: A celebration of the novel that invented the mad scientist, the misunderstood creature and half of modern horror. It is held on its author's birthday.
funFacts: Mary Shelley was born on 30 August 1797 and had written Frankenstein by the age of nineteen.
The story began during the cold, rainy summer of 1816 at Lake Geneva, when the group challenged each other to write ghost stories.
Frankenstein is the scientist, not the creature, which has no name at all in the book.

trail_mix_day.label: National Trail Mix Day
trail_mix_day.intro: Nuts, raisins, seeds and, if nobody is looking, chocolate. The snack that fits in a jacket pocket and makes any walk feel like an expedition.
funFacts: German has had a word for it for centuries: Studentenfutter, student fodder, recorded since the 17th century.
English-speaking hikers often call it gorp, and argue endlessly about what the letters are supposed to stand for.
Nuts and dried fruit keep for months without cooling, which is why the mix travelled long before lightweight packaging existed.
